title: Delhi High Court Questions Police Over Surveillance of CJP Protesters at Jantar Mantar
excerpt: A PIL alleges Delhi Police installed a permanent surveillance tower and indiscriminately filmed protesters — including women in wet clothing — without legal authority, in what the petition calls a violation of constitutional privacy rights.
body:
• Former JNU Students' Union president Aishe Ghosh has filed a PIL in the Delhi High Court challenging what she calls "continuous and intrusive" police surveillance of Cockroach Janta Party protesters at Jantar Mantar.
  • The petition alleges police installed a permanent surveillance tower, photographed routine activities like eating and resting, and threatened to send images to students' parents and colleges.
  • The PIL relies on the Supreme Court's Puttaswamy privacy judgment, arguing the surveillance fails constitutional tests of legality, necessity, and proportionality.
  • The legal challenge comes as tens of thousands of CJP supporters attempted a "Chalo Sansad" march on July 20, the opening day of Parliament's Monsoon Session.

The PIL's Core Claims

Former JNU Students' Union president and CPI(M) leader Aishe Ghosh has moved the Delhi High Court with a public interest litigation alleging that Delhi Police has conducted persistent, indiscriminate surveillance of Cockroach Janta Party protesters and others at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi.

The petition, filed as Aishe Ghosh v. Union of India & Anr, challenges the police's practice of continuously photographing and videographing protesters at the ongoing sit-in and hunger strike, which began on June 20. Central to the complaint is a permanent surveillance tower that Ghosh says was installed at the protest site without any disclosed statutory authority or procedural safeguards.

"On July 20, the opening day of Parliament's Monsoon Session, tens of thousands of CJP supporters gathered at Jantar Mantar for a planned "Chalo Sansad" march toward Parliament."

The surveillance, the petition contends, is not limited to crowd management or security assessments. Ghosh alleges it covers routine activities — eating, resting, and daily life at the protest site — creating conditions that go well beyond reasonable policing of a public assembly.

Chilling Effect on Dissent

One of the petition's most pointed allegations is that police officers threatened some student protesters that their photographs would be shared with their parents and educational institutions. The PIL argues this has created a "chilling effect" that has deterred participation, particularly among younger demonstrators who fear academic or personal repercussions.

The petition also raises concerns about the treatment of women at the site. It alleges that women protesters were photographed and filmed while forced to remain in wet clothing during heavy monsoon rainfall due to inadequate shelter provided at the protest location, calling this "a serious intrusion into bodily privacy and dignity."

"The measures fail the constitutional tests of legality, necessity, and proportionality, violating the rights to privacy, dignity, free speech, and peaceful assembly under Articles 14, 19 and 21."

— From the PIL, citing the Puttaswamy judgment

Legal Framework at Stake

The PIL leans heavily on the Supreme Court's landmark 2017 ruling in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, which established privacy as a fundamental right under the Indian Constitution. Ghosh's petition argues that the police surveillance at Jantar Mantar fails each of the three constitutional tests the Puttaswamy judgment requires for any restriction on privacy: legality, necessity, and proportionality.

Among the reliefs sought are immediate suspension of the surveillance apparatus, full disclosure of the legal basis and data-retention protocols governing the collected footage, preservation of all surveillance records pending adjudication, and the framing of comprehensive guidelines for policing peaceful assemblies across India.

The petition also seeks directions for the provision of basic civic amenities at the protest site, including drinking water and sanitation facilities. It has been filed through advocates Subhash Chandran KR and Anirudh KP.

Wider Context: The Chalo Sansad March

The legal challenge unfolds against the backdrop of an intensifying protest movement. On July 20, the opening day of Parliament's Monsoon Session, tens of thousands of CJP supporters gathered at Jantar Mantar for a planned "Chalo Sansad" march toward Parliament. Delhi Police deployed three-tier security, including paramilitary forces, imposed prohibitory orders banning assemblies of five or more people, and used tear gas and baton charges near Parliament Street to disperse surging crowds.

The government reached out to the movement later in the day, with CJP spokespersons saying they were heading to meet Union Minister J.P. Nadda to present their demands, which center on accountability for exam paper leaks and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Delhi Police has maintained that its security measures, including the surveillance at Jantar Mantar, are aimed at "ensuring law and order, not snooping." The High Court is expected to hear the PIL in the coming days.

nri_angle: The PIL raises questions about protest surveillance and privacy rights in India that resonate with diaspora members who follow Indian civil liberties debates and the CJP movement's anti-corruption demands.
